package_info.package_versions: All versions as of September 2024 (feature abuse, not a code vulnerability)
package_info.why_malicious: The abuse of Entra ID Administrative Units (AUs) enables attackers with privileged access to create persistent, concealed backdoor accounts and covertly assign privileges, making detection and remediation by security teams difficult. This is achieved by leveraging 'restricted management' and 'hidden membership' AU features as intended, but for malicious persistence and privilege escalation.

execution_context.file_location: Microsoft Graph API via Azure CLI or automation (e.g., az rest, Terraform)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
az rest \
  --method post \
  --url https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/directory/administrativeUnits \
  --body '{"displayName": "Sample Administrative Unit", "isMemberManagementRestricted": true}'
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After privilege escalation, the attacker creates a restricted management Administrative Unit (AU) via the Microsoft Graph API, scoping management of AU members to only those with explicit AU-level role assignments, thereby preventing tenant-wide administrators from modifying or deleting AU members.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Creation of a restricted management AU is suspicious when performed by an attacker, as it can be used to lock down backdoor accounts and prevent remediation by global administrators.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, AUs are used for legitimate least-privilege management. Here, the feature is abused to create a persistent, unremovable backdoor account.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use includes protecting executive or sensitive accounts from broad administrative changes.
key_indicators: Creation of AU with isMemberManagementRestricted set to true
AU created by unexpected or recently privileged account
Subsequent addition of suspicious users to the AU

execution_context.file_location: Microsoft Graph API via Azure CLI or automation (e.g., az rest, Terraform)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
az rest \
  --method post \
  --url https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/directory/administrativeUnits \
  --body '{"displayName": "Hidden AU Administrative Unit", "isMemberManagementRestricted": false, "visibility": "HiddenMembership"}'
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After privilege escalation, the attacker creates a hidden membership Administrative Unit (AU) via the Microsoft Graph API, making AU membership invisible to all but a small set of privileged roles, thereby concealing which users are affected by scoped role assignments.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Hidden membership AUs are rarely used and can be abused to conceal the scope of privileged role assignments, making it difficult for security analysts to detect backdoor accounts or privilege escalation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, AU membership should be auditable by security teams. Here, the feature is used to hide the presence of attacker-controlled or targeted accounts.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use includes hiding sensitive group membership for privacy or compliance.
key_indicators: Creation of AU with visibility set to HiddenMembership
AU created by unexpected or recently privileged account
Subsequent role assignments scoped to this AU

execution_context.file_location: Microsoft Graph API via Azure CLI or automation (e.g., az rest, Terraform)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After creating a restricted or hidden membership AU, the attacker adds a backdoor account as a member, ensuring that only scoped AU administrators can manage the account, and/or that the account's presence is concealed from most administrators.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Adding a suspicious or new account to a restricted or hidden AU is a strong indicator of privilege persistence or concealment.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, AU membership changes are transparent and auditable. Here, the attacker is using the AU to shield the backdoor account from detection and remediation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Adding legitimate users to AUs for delegated administration.
key_indicators: Addition of new or suspicious user to restricted/hidden AU
Timing correlation with AU creation and role assignment

execution_context.file_location: Microsoft Graph API via Azure CLI or automation (e.g., az rest, Terraform)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: After creating a hidden membership AU and adding target users, the attacker assigns a privileged role (e.g., Privileged Authentication Administrator) to the backdoor account, scoped only to the hidden AU, enabling covert privilege escalation and account takeover.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Scoped role assignments to hidden AUs are rare and can be used to grant powerful privileges to attacker-controlled accounts without detection.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, privileged role assignments are visible and auditable. Here, the attacker is hiding the scope and impact of the assignment.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Delegating limited admin rights to helpdesk or regional admins.
key_indicators: Role assignment scoped to hidden AU
Assignment of high-privilege roles to new or suspicious accounts

attack_chain.action: Attacker with privileged access creates a restricted management AU to shield backdoor accounts from tenant-wide admin actions.
attack_chain.leads_to: Step 2: Add attacker-controlled account to the restricted AU.

attack_chain.action: Attacker adds a backdoor account as a member of the restricted management AU, making it unmodifiable by global admins.
attack_chain.leads_to: Step 3: (Optional) Create a hidden membership AU for covert privilege assignment.

attack_chain.action: Attacker creates a hidden membership AU to conceal the scope of privileged role assignments.
attack_chain.leads_to: Step 4: Assign privileged roles to the backdoor account scoped to the hidden AU.

attack_chain.action: Attacker assigns a privileged role (e.g., Privileged Authentication Administrator) to the backdoor account, scoped to the hidden AU, enabling covert account takeover and persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Final goal: Persistent, concealed privileged access and ability to take over sensitive accounts.

behavioral_signatures: Creation of Administrative Units with isMemberManagementRestricted or visibility: HiddenMembership
Addition of users to restricted or hidden AUs
Scoped role assignments to hidden or restricted AUs
Failed admin actions (e.g., password reset, delete) on users in restricted AUs
network_indicators: Microsoft Graph API calls to /directory/administrativeUnits and /roleManagement/directory/roleAssignments
Azure CLI (az rest) or automation tool activity creating or modifying AUs
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Entra ID audit logs for creation or modification of Administrative Units, especially those with isMemberManagementRestricted or visibility: HiddenMembership. Alert on addition of users to these AUs and on role assignments scoped to them. Correlate failed admin actions (e.g., password reset, delete) with AU membership. Review all scoped role assignments and AU membership changes, and investigate any AUs that appear empty in the portal but have recent activity in logs. Train analysts to recognize that hidden AUs may not display members in the portal and to use logs for verification.
